contents.text: A food chain is a model. A model can be used to represent events in nature and make these events easier to understand. A food chain is a model that shows where organisms in an ecosystem get their food.
A food chain has arrows that point from one organism to another. Each arrow shows the direction that matter moves when one organism eats another organism.

Matter enters a food chain when a producer makes its own food. This is how all of the matter eaten by organisms enters the food chain. Many producers make their own food using carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight. Producers do not eat other organisms, so there is no arrow pointing from another organism to the producer in a food chain.
Matter first moves up a food chain when the producer is eaten by a consumer. This is shown by an arrow pointing from the producer to a consumer.
A consumer that hunts and eats another consumer is a predator. The consumer eaten by a predator is its prey. Matter moves up a food chain when a predator hunts and eats its prey.

contents.text: Use the arrows to figure out how matter moves in this food chain.
There is no arrow pointing to the bear sedge in this food chain. The bear sedge does not eat other organisms. It makes its own food. The bear sedge is the producer.
An arrow shows that the bear sedge is eaten by the brown lemming.
So, the producer in this food chain is the bear sedge. It is eaten by the brown lemming.

Matter first moves up a food chain when the producer is eaten by a consumer. This is shown by an arrow pointing from the producer to a consumer.

pieces.text: Alpheid shrimp are small crustaceans that build
, or underground shelters, in the sand. Alpheid shrimp are blind, so they are vulnerable to predators when they leave their burrows.

textContent.text: A shrimp may allow a fish to share its burrow. This fish, called a goby, acts as a lookout for the blind shrimp. When the shrimp goes outside, it touches its antennae to the goby's tail. If a predator comes near, the goby flicks its tail, alerting the shrimp to the danger. Both animals then retreat to the safety of the burrow.

textContent.text: A rat tapeworm is a type of flatworm that can live inside a rat's body. When a rat eats an insect that has a tapeworm inside it, the insect is digested, but the tapeworm remains alive.

The tapeworm is moved into the rat's intestines and uses suckers to attach itself to the intestine wall. Inside the rat's intestine, the tapeworm absorbs nutrients from food that the rat has eaten. If the rat has many tapeworms in its intestines, it will become weak from lack of nutrients.

textContent.text: Tropical pitcher plants live in soil that is poor in nutrients. To get the nutrients it needs to survive, the plant uses a pitcher-shaped leaf as a trap to catch and digest small organisms. But the plant can also get nutrients from other sources, including from the feces of woolly bats.

pieces.text: A woolly bat can

, or settle to sleep, in the upper part of the plant's trap. In the trap, the bat is protected from predators and bad weather. When the bat roosts, it can drop waste, including feces, into the bottom of the trap. The bottom of the trap holds a liquid that helps the plant digest the feces. The plant then absorbs nutrients from the digested feces.

textContent.text: Tropical pitcher plants live in soil that is poor in nutrients. To get the nutrients it needs to survive, the plant uses a pitcher-shaped leaf as a trap to catch and digest small organisms. But the plant can also get nutrients from other sources, including from the feces of woolly bats.

pieces.text: A woolly bat can

, or settle to sleep, in the upper part of the plant's trap. In the trap, the bat is protected from predators and bad weather. When the bat roosts, it can drop waste, including feces, into the bottom of the trap. The bottom of the trap holds a liquid that helps the plant digest the feces. The plant then absorbs nutrients from the digested feces.

lessons.name: Investigate primary succession on a volcanic island

pieces.text: Before sunrise on November 14, 1963, the crew of the fishing boat

had just finished putting their lines in the ocean off the southern coast of Iceland. As the crew waited to have breakfast, a strong smell of sulfur drifted over the boat. At first, crew members thought that the cook had burned the eggs or that something was wrong with the boat's engine. But when the sun started to rise, the crew saw black smoke billowing from the water a few kilometers away.
The captain of the
assumed the smoke was coming from a boat that was on fire, so he sailed closer to try to help. As the

approached the smoke, the surface of the sea grew rough. The captain and crew saw flashes of lightning in the column of smoke and glowing pieces of molten rock shooting up out of the water. The captain realized this was not a burning boat. It was a volcano erupting under the water!

contents.text: The volcano continued to erupt. By November 20, 1963—just six days after the volcano first erupted—it had produced enough lava and ash to form an island that rose 70 meters above the ocean's surface. The volcano finally stopped erupting in 1967. By then, the island had grown to 2.65 square kilometers, and its highest point was 175 meters above sea level.

This newly formed island, called Surtsey, is located 33 kilometers off the southern coast of Iceland. Surtsey has a cold, harsh environment. In the winter, the temperature is often just above freezing, and in the summer, it rarely gets above 50℉. Surtsey is also a very windy place. High winds near the island help create large waves that scour the coastline.

pieces.text: When the island of Surtsey first formed, it was

, which means that it did not have any living organisms on it. Hot rocks and ash covered the island's surface, and toxic gas and lava flowed out of the volcano. After the volcano stopped erupting, organisms started to live and grow on Surtsey. The number and type of organisms that lived on the island changed over time in a process called succession.

pieces.text: Seeds from many species of plants drifted on ocean currents from Iceland to Surtsey. But only some of these plants were able to
, or move onto and reproduce on, the new island. These species of plants are examples of pioneer species. A
is an organism that can colonize either a new environment or an environment where the ecosystem was destroyed.

contents.text: Pioneer species have traits that allow them to survive in environments that are too harsh for most species. The traits that allow a pioneer species to colonize a new environment depend on the conditions of that environment.

To have been a pioneer species on Surtsey, seeds needed to germinate and grow in rocky soil with few nutrients. Most of the seeds that arrived on Surtsey did not have traits that allowed them to be pioneer species there.

had just finished putting their lines in the ocean off the southern coast of Iceland. As the crew waited to have breakfast, a strong smell of sulfur drifted over the boat. At first, crew members thought that the cook had burned the eggs or that something was wrong with the boat's engine. But when the sun started to rise, the crew saw black smoke billowing from the water a few kilometers away.
The captain of the
assumed the smoke was coming from a boat that was on fire, so he sailed closer to try to help. As the

approached the smoke, the surface of the sea grew rough. The captain and crew saw flashes of lightning in the column of smoke and glowing pieces of molten rock shooting up out of the water. The captain realized this was not a burning boat. It was a volcano erupting under the water!

contents.text: The volcano continued to erupt. By November 20, 1963—just six days after the volcano first erupted—it had produced enough lava and ash to form an island that rose 70 meters above the ocean's surface. The volcano finally stopped erupting in 1967. By then, the island had grown to 2.65 square kilometers, and its highest point was 175 meters above sea level.

This newly formed island, called Surtsey, is located 33 kilometers off the southern coast of Iceland. Surtsey has a cold, harsh environment. In the winter, the temperature is often just above freezing, and in the summer, it rarely gets above 50℉. Surtsey is also a very windy place. High winds near the island help create large waves that scour the coastline.

pieces.text: Before sunrise on November 14, 1963, the crew of the fishing boat

had just finished putting their lines in the ocean off the southern coast of Iceland. As the crew waited to have breakfast, a strong smell of sulfur drifted over the boat. At first, crew members thought that the cook had burned the eggs or that something was wrong with the boat's engine. But when the sun started to rise, the crew saw black smoke billowing from the water a few kilometers away.
The captain of the
assumed the smoke was coming from a boat that was on fire, so he sailed closer to try to help. As the

approached the smoke, the surface of the sea grew rough. The captain and crew saw flashes of lightning in the column of smoke and glowing pieces of molten rock shooting up out of the water. The captain realized this was not a burning boat. It was a volcano erupting under the water!

contents.text: The volcano continued to erupt. By November 20, 1963—just six days after the volcano first erupted—it had produced enough lava and ash to form an island that rose 70 meters above the ocean's surface. The volcano finally stopped erupting in 1967. By then, the island had grown to 2.65 square kilometers, and its highest point was 175 meters above sea level.

This newly formed island, called Surtsey, is located 33 kilometers off the southern coast of Iceland. Surtsey has a cold, harsh environment. In the winter, the temperature is often just above freezing, and in the summer, it rarely gets above 50℉. Surtsey is also a very windy place. High winds near the island help create large waves that scour the coastline.

When Surtsey first formed, it was sterile and covered with new rock, so its soil had few nutrients. So, the ability to germinate in rocky soil with few nutrients would help a seed successfully colonize the island.

content.text: the ability to survive cold temperatures

explanationText.text: Surtsey has a cold, harsh environment. In the winter, the temperature is often just above freezing, and in the summer, it rarely gets above 50℉. So, the ability to survive cold temperatures would help a seed successfully colonize the island.

content.text: the ability to stick to fur or hair

explanationText.text: Some seeds can be transported to a new place by sticking to fur or hair. But no animals with fur or hair lived on Surtsey. So, the ability to stick to fur or hair would not help a seed successfully colonize the island.

contents.text: In order for a plant to be a pioneer species on Surtsey, a seed from that plant had to travel to the island. Then, the plant that grew from the seed had to survive long enough to reproduce.
First, the plant's seed needed to enter the ocean.
Next, the seed had to survive its journey drifting to Surtsey on ocean currents.
Then, the seed had to be able to germinate, or sprout, and grow in rocky soil with few nutrients.
Finally, the seedling that grew from the seed had to survive the harsh environment on Surtsey so the plant could grow and reproduce.

pieces.text: Before sunrise on November 14, 1963, the crew of the fishing boat

had just finished putting their lines in the ocean off the southern coast of Iceland. As the crew waited to have breakfast, a strong smell of sulfur drifted over the boat. At first, crew members thought that the cook had burned the eggs or that something was wrong with the boat's engine. But when the sun started to rise, the crew saw black smoke billowing from the water a few kilometers away.
The captain of the
assumed the smoke was coming from a boat that was on fire, so he sailed closer to try to help. As the

approached the smoke, the surface of the sea grew rough. The captain and crew saw flashes of lightning in the column of smoke and glowing pieces of molten rock shooting up out of the water. The captain realized this was not a burning boat. It was a volcano erupting under the water!

contents.text: The volcano continued to erupt. By November 20, 1963—just six days after the volcano first erupted—it had produced enough lava and ash to form an island that rose 70 meters above the ocean's surface. The volcano finally stopped erupting in 1967. By then, the island had grown to 2.65 square kilometers, and its highest point was 175 meters above sea level.

This newly formed island, called Surtsey, is located 33 kilometers off the southern coast of Iceland. Surtsey has a cold, harsh environment. In the winter, the temperature is often just above freezing, and in the summer, it rarely gets above 50℉. Surtsey is also a very windy place. High winds near the island help create large waves that scour the coastline.

explanationText.text: Primary succession is the process of organisms beginning to live and grow in an environment that was sterile. A sterile environment does not have any living organisms in it. Surtsey was sterile when it first formed, so it was a good place to study primary succession.

the volcano stopped erupting. Up until that point, the island was sterile because the eruption prevented organisms from surviving. So, this statement is not true.

content.text: The government of Iceland protected the island from being disturbed much by human visitors.

explanationText.text: Human visitors could bring organisms to Surtsey that otherwise could not have reached the island. Those organisms could change how primary succession happens on Surtsey. But the government of Iceland has protected the island from being disturbed much by human visitors. So, scientists can study how primary succession happens without wondering if the organisms they observe are there because of human interference.
